title: Definition of Probability Measure
text:
2. Definition
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space. A set function \(P: \mathcal{F} \to [0, 1]\) is called a probability measure if it satisfies the following conditions:

\(P(\Omega) = 1\).
(Countable Additivity) For any pairwise disjoint sequence of events \(\{E_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathcal{F}\), \[
P\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n \right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty P(E_n)
\]

title: Definition of Probability Measure

3. Example
If we consider a fair coin toss, \(\Omega = \{H, T\}\) and \(P(\{H\}) = P(\{T\}) = 0.5\).

NoteExercise 1.13



Suppose X(t) is a stochastic process with stationary independent increments that satisfies E[X(1)]=0, E[X(1)^2]=1, and 
X(t) \sim \sqrt{t}X(1) \quad \text{for } t \ge 0.
 Use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to show that X(t) - X(s) follows N(0, |t-s|) for s,t \ge 0.



Proof. Proof.
Let s < t. Since X has stationary independent increments, X(t) - X(s) has the same distribution as X(t-s). By the scaling property given in the problem, 
X(t-s) \sim \sqrt{t-s}X(1).
 Therefore, it suffices to show that X(1) \sim N(0,1).
Fix n \in \mathbb{N}. We can decompose X(1) into a sum of n independent increments: 
X(1) = \sum_{k=1}^n \left( X\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) - X\left(\frac{k-1}{n}\right) \right).
 Let Y_{n,k} = X(\frac{k}{n}) - X(\frac{k-1}{n}). Due to stationary independent increments, Y_{n,k} are i.i.d. variables distributed as X(1/n). Using the scaling property X(1/n) \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}X(1), we have: 
E[Y_{n,k}] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}E[X(1)] = 0, \quad \text{Var}(Y_{n,k}) = \frac{1}{n}\text{Var}(X(1)) = \frac{1}{n}.
